This accomplishment not only underscores the technical success of the project but also highlights its potential scalability and applicability in industrial settings, offering a sustainable alternative to traditional chemical synthesis methods. Path Forward Electrochemical Conversion MSU demonstrated successful sintering of multiple large-scale FTC tin membranes with the warranty-repaired furnace, demonstrating the ability to scale this challenging material (Figure 39). Further, we also showed success in creating hydrophobic surfaces with aerosol spraying PTFE treatments on the tin to prevent ingress/flooding of the catholyte solution (Figure 40), achieving a ready state to test and optimize the systems in a catalytic framework, including degradation. PTFE aerosol spray treatments showing the progression of wetting to non-wetting OCOchem will continue to scale up the reactor to industrial sizes (>1.5 m2 or 15,000 cm2 with a height of 1.2 m and width >1.3 m), applying the learning from this project. OCOchem will also develop hydrodynamics with operating conditions and GDE modifications to obtain sustained uniform reactions at the gas-liquid-solid interface of such large-sized reactor cells, which is necessary for the commercial feasibility of CO 2 electrolysis technology. Biological Upconversion Moving forward, our research aims to optimize the co-feeding of formate and formaldehyde under anaerobic conditions in a 0.5L fermenter. Based on our current data, we anticipate that this method could significantly enhance the ethylene glycol titer. One of the major challenges in commercializing this technology is the difficulty cells face in sustaining long-term catalytic production of ethylene glycol. To address this, our future efforts will focus on cell encapsulation or cell immobilization techniques within the context of resting cell bioconversion. By enclosing the cells in a semi-permeable matrix or membrane, we aim to improve the stability and reusability of the biocatalysts, thereby extending their catalytic life. After these studies, we plan to consider filing for a patent, marking a significant step towards the potential commercialization of this technology. Additionally, we will assess the scalability of the process and identify any remaining technical risks, such as metabolic burden or potential impacts of excess product accumulation. While by-product toxicity has not been a primary concern so far, the effect of high concentrations of desired products on cell health and productivity is still unclear. As we move towards industrial application, understanding and mitigating these issues will be crucial to ensuring the viability and efficiency of the bioconversion process in larger-scale operations.
